name: Hesiod on the race of iron
text: For now truly is a race of iron, and men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, and from perishing by night; and the gods shall lay sore trouble upon them. ... There will be no favour for the man who keeps his oath or for the just or for the good; but rather men will praise the evil-doer and his violent dealing.
author: Hesiod
witness: A Boeotian farmer-poet writing around 700 BCE, four centuries after the palaces fell. His age of heroes and age of iron are myth, not memory of 1177, but they show how Iron Age Greeks imagined a lost, better past. Discount the moralising; Hesiod is complaining about his own brother and corrupt local lords.

name: Herodotus on Meroe
text: you will come to a great city called Meroe. This city is said to be the mother-city of all the other Ethiopians: and they who dwell in it reverence of the gods Zeus and Dionysos alone, and these they greatly honour; and they have an Oracle of Zeus established
author: Herodotus
witness: Herodotus never went beyond Elephantine; this is hearsay from Egyptian informants. 'Zeus and Dionysos' are his Greek names for Amun and probably Osiris or a Kushite god. Still the earliest Greek notice of Meroe as a great city, in the fifth century BCE.

name: The Daodejing on wanting more
text: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
author: Laozi (attributed)
witness: A text compiled over the fourth and third centuries BCE and attributed to a figure who may be legendary; Legge's 1891 Victorian translation adds his own Christian vocabulary. The praise of contentment and few desires is exactly the 'ascetic wisdom' that Baumard and colleagues tie to rising affluence.

name: Arrian on the burning of Persepolis
text: He burnt down the Persian palace, though Parmenio advised him to preserve it, for many reasons, and especially because it was not well to destroy what was now his own property, and because the men of Asia would not by this course of action be induced to come over to him, thinking that he himself had decided not to retain the rule of Asia, but only to conquer it and depart. But Alexander said that he wished to take vengeance on the Persians, in retaliation for their deeds in the invasion of Greece
author: Arrian
witness: Arrian wrote under Hadrian, about 450 years later, from the lost memoirs of Ptolemy and Aristobulus, both Alexander's officers and both inclined to flatter him. Other writers blame a drunken party. Note Parmenio's argument: burning the palace told Persians he would not rule as their king, the very policy Alexander then adopted.

name: Ammianus on the coming of the Huns
text: The following circumstances were the original cause of all the destruction and various calamities which the fury of Mars roused up, throwing everything into confusion by his usual ruinous violence: the people called Huns, slightly mentioned in the ancient records, live beyond the Sea of Azov, on the border of the Frozen Ocean, and are a race savage beyond all parallel.
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
witness: A Greek-speaking officer from Antioch writing in Rome around 390, a contemporary of Adrianople. He had never seen the Huns; his ethnography follows classical stereotypes of steppe 'savages'. But he is the key witness for Heather's view that the Huns set the whole chain in motion.

name: Ammianus on the Danube crossing of 376
text: Moreover, having obtained permission of the emperor to cross the Danube and to cultivate some districts in Thrace, they crossed the stream day and night, without ceasing, embarking in troops on board ships and rafts, and canoes made of the hollow trunks of trees
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
witness: Written fifteen years later by a retired officer who blamed greedy Roman generals for the disaster that followed. His point that the Goths were admitted by imperial permission is the basis of Halsall's and Kulikowski's emphasis on Roman policy; his claim that their numbers could not be counted is a literary topos.

name: Ammianus on the slaughter at Adrianople
text: Scarcely one-third of the whole army escaped. ... Nor, except the battle of Cannæ, is so destructive a slaughter recorded in our annals
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
witness: Ammianus ends his whole history with Adrianople, which tells you how he saw it. The comparison with Cannae is rhetorical; the real Roman losses are unknown, perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 men. He was writing for a Roman senatorial audience who knew their Livy.

name: Jerome hears of the sack of Rome
text: My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken; ... famine was beforehand with the sword and but few citizens were left to be made captives.
author: Jerome
witness: Written in Bethlehem, far from Rome, in a letter of consolation about the noblewoman Marcella. Jerome had news from refugees and frames the sack with biblical laments. It shows the shock to the Roman elite; it is not an eyewitness account of what the Goths did.

name: Augustine on why he wrote The City of God
text: Rome having been stormed and sacked by the Goths under Alaric their king, ... the worshippers of false gods, or pagans, as we commonly call them, made an attempt to attribute this calamity to the Christian religion, and began to blaspheme the true God with even more than their wonted bitterness and acerbity.
author: Augustine of Hippo
work: Retractations II.43, quoted in the editor's preface to The City of God
witness: Augustine looking back late in life, as bishop of Hippo in Africa. He confirms that pagans blamed Christianity for Rome's fall within months of 410, the argument Gibbon revived; his answer, that the earthly city always passes, shaped Western thought for a millennium.

name: Procopius on the plague in Constantinople
text: Now the disease in Byzantium ran a course of four months, and its greatest virulence lasted about three. And at first the deaths were a little more than the normal, then the mortality rose still higher, and afterwards the tale of dead reached five thousand each day, and again it even came to ten thousand and still more than that.
author: Procopius
witness: An eyewitness in the capital, secretary to Belisarius, writing in the 540s and modelling his account on Thucydides' plague of Athens. The daily death counts are guesses; minimalists such as Mordechai and Eisenberg doubt the empire-wide scale that maximalists read into them.

name: Procopius on the dim sun of 536
text: For the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse, for the beams it shed were not clear nor such as it is accustomed to shed. And from the time when this thing happened men were free neither from war nor pestilence nor any other thing leading to death.
author: Procopius
witness: Procopius was in the West with Belisarius in 536. Ice cores and tree rings now confirm a huge volcanic dust veil in 536 and another in 539-540, which makes this one of the best-corroborated sentences in ancient history. The moral link to war and pestilence is his own framing.

name: The Periplus on the ivory road to Adulis
text: inland from this a three days' journey is a city, Kolöê, the first market where ivory can be procured. From Kolöê it takes a journey of five days to reach the metropolis of the people called the Auxumitae, whereto is brought, through the province called Kyêneion, all the ivory obtained on the other side of the Nile, before it is sent on to Adouli.
author: Anonymous Greek merchant
witness: A practical guide by a Greek-speaking trader from Roman Egypt, written in the mid first century CE. It is the earliest text to name Aksum. Its point that ivory from 'the other side of the Nile' was routed to Adulis is the heart of the trade-shift argument for Meroe's decline.

name: Gibbon on immoderate greatness
text: But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the causes of destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest; and as soon as time or accident had removed the artificial supports, the stupendous fabric yielded to the pressure of its own weight.
author: Edward Gibbon
work: Decline and Fall, General Observations on the Fall of the Roman Empire in the West
witness: Not an ancient source but the founding text of the modern debate, written in the 1770s and 1780s by an English Enlightenment historian who disliked the church. Read it as the classic statement of the internal-decay school, which Heather argues against.

name: Gibbon on why Constantinople survived
text: Yet the salutary event approved in some measure the judgment of Constantine. During a long period of decay, his impregnable city repelled the victorious armies of Barbarians, protected the wealth of Asia, and commanded, both in peace and war, the important straits which connect the Euxine and Mediterranean Seas. The foundation of Constantinople more essentially contributed to the preservation of the East, than to the ruin of the West.
author: Edward Gibbon
work: Decline and Fall, General Observations on the Fall of the Roman Empire in the West
witness: Gibbon's answer to Rishi's question in one paragraph: walls, the wealth of Asia and the straits. Modern historians keep all three and add the East's richer tax base, its diplomacy and its institutions.
